title: Create an IAM user with no permissions and test listing S3
goal: Goal: Create an IAM user with no permissions, configure AWS CLI credentials for that user, run aws s3 ls, and confirm the expected AccessDenied result.

concepts.title: IAM user
concepts.body: A long-term identity inside one AWS account.

concepts.title: No permissions
concepts.body: The user exists but cannot do AWS actions.

concepts.title: Implicit deny
concepts.body: AWS denies actions unless a policy allows them.

concepts.title: Access key

whyItMatters: IAM starts with no permissions. This lab proves that a user existing in AWS is not enough to perform actions. An allow policy must apply, otherwise AWS returns an implicit deny.

title: Attach AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess and re-test
goal: Goal: Attach the AWS managed policy AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess to the no-permissions IAM user from task 1, then verify S3 read/list actions work while write actions remain denied.

concepts.title: AWS managed policy
concepts.body: A policy created and maintained by AWS, such as AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess.

concepts.title: Read-only does not mean write
concepts.body: The user can list and read S3 data but should not upload, delete, or modify objects.

concepts.title: Policy attachment
concepts.body: Attaching a policy to a user gives that identity the policy permissions.

concepts.title: Inherited permissions
concepts.body: A user can receive permissions directly, from groups, or through other policy types.

concepts.title: Explicit deny still wins
concepts.body: A deny from another policy can still block an action even when this managed policy allows it.

concepts.title: Exam clue
concepts.body: Managed policies are fast for labs, but least-privilege custom policies are often better for production.

whyItMatters: This builds directly on task 1. The same user moved from implicit deny to allowed S3 read/list access because an allow policy was attached.

title: Custom identity-based policy for one S3 bucket
goal: Goal: Create one S3 bucket, one IAM user, and a custom identity-based policy that allows s3:ListBucket only on that one bucket. Then verify the user cannot list all buckets, read objects, write objects, or access another bucket.

concepts.title: Identity-based policy
concepts.body: A policy attached to a user, group, or role. It says what that identity can do.

concepts.title: Bucket-level action
concepts.body: s3:ListBucket works on the bucket ARN, such as arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name.

concepts.title: No account-wide listing
concepts.body: s3:ListAllMyBuckets is separate. Without it, the user cannot list every bucket in the account.

concepts.title: No object access
concepts.body: s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject need object ARNs such as arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/*. This lab does not grant them.

concepts.title: Implicit deny
concepts.body: Anything not allowed is denied by default unless another policy allows it.

concepts.title: Least privilege
concepts.body: The policy allows exactly one action on exactly one bucket resource.

whyItMatters: This is least privilege in a small, testable form. The user can list the contents of one named bucket, but cannot discover all buckets, access objects, upload objects, or access another bucket.
costWarning: IAM users and customer managed IAM policies have no direct charge. Empty S3 buckets have no storage charge, but object storage and requests can cost money. This lab uses empty buckets; still delete the buckets, access keys, policy, and user when finished.

instructions.text: Sign in to the AWS Management Console as an administrator or a lab role with IAM and S3 permissions.
Set the console region to eu-west-2 for the S3 bucket creation pages.
Open your AWS account ID from the account menu or use the CLI command in the CLI path later.

consoleSteps.title: Create the allowed S3 bucket

instructions.text: Use bucket name iam-task-3-allowed-bucket-[account-id], replacing [account-id] with your AWS account ID.

consoleSteps.note: S3 bucket names are globally unique. Adding your account ID makes the name much less likely to clash.

consoleSteps.title: Create the optional blocked bucket

instructions.text: Create a second empty bucket named iam-task-3-blocked-bucket-[account-id] in eu-west-2.
This bucket is only for proving that the test user cannot list another bucket.

consoleSteps.warning: Do not put real data in either lab bucket.

consoleSteps.title: Create the IAM user

instructions.text: Set the user name to iam-task-3-user.
Do not give console access for this lab.
On permissions, choose to create the user with no permissions for now.

consoleSteps.note: The user starts with no access. The custom policy will be the only permission you add.

consoleSteps.title: Create the custom identity-based policy

instructions.text: Paste the policy below, replacing [account-id] in the bucket ARN with your real account ID.

consoleSteps.warning: The policy allows only s3:ListBucket on the allowed bucket ARN. Do not add s3:ListAllMyBuckets, s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, or /*.

consoleSteps.title: Attach the policy to the user
consoleSteps.note: This makes it an identity-based policy because it is attached to the IAM user identity.

consoleSteps.title: Create access keys for testing

instructions.text: Open the Security credentials tab for iam-task-3-user.
Create an access key for CLI use.
Store the access key ID and secret access key only in your local lab environment.
Configure them as a CLI profile named iam-task-3-user.

consoleSteps.warning: Access keys are credentials. Do not commit them, screenshot them, or leave them active after the lab.

consoleSteps.title: Verify allowed and denied access

instructions.text: Using the test user's CLI profile, list the allowed bucket. This should succeed.
Try to list all buckets. This should fail because s3:ListAllMyBuckets is not allowed.
Try to list the blocked bucket. This should fail because the resource ARN is not allowed.
Try to upload or download an object. This should fail because object actions are not allowed.

consoleSteps.note: A successful lab has one success and several expected access denied results.

consoleSteps.title: Tear down in dependency order

instructions.text: Delete any test objects if you created any.
Delete the optional blocked S3 bucket.
Delete the access key for iam-task-3-user.
Delete the customer managed policy IAMTask3ListOnlyOneBucketPolicy.

consoleSteps.warning: Delete the user attachment before deleting the policy. Delete bucket contents before deleting buckets.

title: Add an explicit Deny statement and confirm it overrides Allow
goal: Goal: Prove the IAM rule that Explicit Deny always wins, even if another policy says Allow.

concepts.title: Explicit deny
concepts.body: A Deny statement that matches the request blocks it.

concepts.title: Allow
concepts.body: An Allow works only when no explicit deny applies.

concepts.title: Implicit deny
concepts.body: Default result when no allow matches.

concepts.title: Policy simulator

concepts.title: Bucket-level action
concepts.body: s3:ListBucket uses the bucket ARN.

concepts.title: Deny locations
concepts.body: Denies can appear in identity policies, resource policies, SCPs, boundaries, or session policies.

whyItMatters: This is one of the most tested IAM rules. When access should work but fails, look for an explicit deny before assuming the allow policy is wrong.
costWarning: IAM policies have no extra cost. The CLI tests do not create storage. Delete the deny policy after testing so it does not affect later labs.

instructions.text: Sign in to AWS as admin.

ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
echo $ACCOUNT_ID
aws iam create-saml-provider --name CorpIDP --saml-metadata-document file://idp-metadata.xml

aws iam create-role --role-name SAMLReadRole --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name SAMLReadRole --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess

RUNTIME="python3.12"

VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=isDefault,Values=true --query "Vpcs[0].VpcId" --output text)
SUBNET_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=default-for-az,Values=true --query "Subnets[0].SubnetId" --output text)
SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name "$SG_NAME" --description "SG for IAM Task 25" --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 create-key-pair --key-name "$KEY_NAME" --query KeyMaterial --output text > "$KEY_NAME.pem"
chmod 400 "$KEY_NAME.pem"
AMI_ID=$(aws ssm get-parameter --name /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 --query Parameter.Value --output text)

TAGGED_ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --image-id "$AMI_ID" --instance-type t3.micro --key-name "$KEY_NAME" --security-group-ids "$SG_ID" --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" --tag-specifications "ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=tagged-instance},{Key=$TAG_KEY,Value=$TAG_VALUE}]" --query "Instances[0].InstanceId" --output text)
UNTAGGED_ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --image-id "$AMI_ID" --instance-type t3.micro --key-name "$KEY_NAME" --security-group-ids "$SG_ID" --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" --tag-specifications "ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=untagged-instance}]" --query "Instances[0].InstanceId" --output text)
aws ec2 wait instance-running --instance-ids "$TAGGED_ID" "$UNTAGGED_ID"

cat > trust.json <<'JSON'
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"lambda.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}
JSON
aws iam create-role --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole
cat > manage-tagged-ec2.json <<'JSON'
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Sid":"DescribeInstances","Effect":"Allow","Action":"ec2:DescribeInstances","Resource":"*"},{"Sid":"StopOnlyTagged","Effect":"Allow","Action":"ec2:StopInstances","Resource":"arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*","Condition":{"StringEquals":{"ec2:ResourceTag/AutoStop":"true"}}}]}
JSON
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --policy-name ManageTaggedEc2 --policy-document file://manage-tagged-ec2.json

aws lambda invoke --function-name "$FUNC_NAME" --payload '{"mode":"stop"}' response.json
cat response.json
aws lambda invoke --function-name "$FUNC_NAME" --payload "{"mode":"stop","untagged_instance_id":"$UNTAGGED_ID"}" response2.json
cat response2.json
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids "$TAGGED_ID" "$UNTAGGED_ID" --query "Reservations[].Instances[].{Id:InstanceId,State:State.Name,Name:Tags[?Key=='Name']|[0].Value,AutoStop:Tags[?Key=='AutoStop']|[0].Value}" --output table

cliSteps.title: Tear down in dependency order

commands.text:
aws lambda delete-function --function-name "$FUNC_NAME"
aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --policy-name ManageTaggedEc2
aws iam detach-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole
aws iam delete-role --role-name "$ROLE_NAME"
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids "$TAGGED_ID" "$UNTAGGED_ID"
aws ec2 wait instance-terminated --instance-ids "$TAGGED_ID" "$UNTAGGED_ID"
aws ec2 delete-security-group --group-id "$SG_ID"
aws ec2 delete-key-pair --key-name "$KEY_NAME"
rm -f "$KEY_NAME.pem" trust.json manage-tagged-ec2.json lambda_function.py function.zip response.json response2.json
